claim: The NLRP1 inflammasome is a multiprotein complex that is a potent activator of inflammation.
source: The NLRP1 inflammasome is a multiprotein complex that is a potent activator of inflammation.
evidence: This is a general statement about NLRP1 function that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Mouse NLRP1B can be activated through proteolytic cleavage by the bacterial Lethal Toxin (LeTx) protease.
source: Mouse NLRP1B can be activated through proteolytic cleavage by the bacterial Lethal Toxin (LeTx) protease, resulting in degradation of the N-terminal domains of NLRP1B and liberation of the bioactive C-terminal domain, which includes the caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage by LeTx results in degradation of the N-terminal domains of NLRP1B and liberation of the bioactive C-terminal domain containing CARD.
source: Mouse NLRP1B can be activated through proteolytic cleavage by the bacterial Lethal Toxin (LeTx) protease, resulting in degradation of the N-terminal domains of NLRP1B and liberation of the bioactive C-terminal domain, which includes the caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of NLRP1B activation by LeTx, supported by prior research.

claim: Natural pathogen-derived effectors that can activate human NLRP1 have remained unknown prior to this study.
source: However, natural pathogen-derived effectors that can activate human NLRP1 have remained unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Several proteases from diverse picornaviruses cleave human NLRP1 within a rapidly evolving region of the protein.
source: Here, we use an evolutionary model to identify several proteases from diverse picornaviruses that cleave human NLRP1 within a rapidly evolving region of the protein, leading to host-specific and virus-specific activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cleavage of human NLRP1 by picornavirus proteases leads to host-specific and virus-specific activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome.
source: Here, we use an evolutionary model to identify several proteases from diverse picornaviruses that cleave human NLRP1 within a rapidly evolving region of the protein, leading to host-specific and virus-specific activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: NLRP1 acts as a 'tripwire' to recognize the enzymatic function of a wide range of viral proteases.
source: Our work demonstrates that NLRP1 acts as a 'tripwire' to recognize the enzymatic function of a wide range of viral proteases and suggests that host mimicry of viral polyprotein cleavage sites can be an evolutionary strategy to activate a robust inflammatory immune response.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Host mimicry of viral polyprotein cleavage sites can be an evolutionary strategy to activate a robust inflammatory immune response.
source: Our work demonstrates that NLRP1 acts as a 'tripwire' to recognize the enzymatic function of a wide range of viral proteases and suggests that host mimicry of viral polyprotein cleavage sites can be an evolutionary strategy to activate a robust inflammatory immune response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings that involves inference about evolutionary strategy.

claim: Innate immune sensors detect broadly conserved microbial molecules such as bacterial flagellin or double-stranded RNA.
source: To ensure accurate discrimination of self and non-self, innate immune sensors detect broadly conserved microbial molecules such as bacterial flagellin or double-stranded RNA (Janeway, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pathogen-specific activities such as toxins or effector enzymes have been shown to be targets of innate immune recognition.
source: More recently, pathogen-specific activities such as toxins or effector enzymes have also been shown to be targets of innate immune recognition (Jones et al., 2016; Mitchell et al., 2019; Vance et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Effector-triggered immunity (ETI) has been well-established in plants.
source: Such a system for detection, termed effector-trigged immunity (ETI), has been well-established in plants (Cui et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2016) and is emerging as an important means to allow the immune system to distinguish pathogens from harmless microbes in animals (Fischer et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Effector-triggered immunity is emerging as an important means to allow the immune system to distinguish pathogens from harmless microbes in animals.
source: Such a system for detection, termed effector-trigged immunity (ETI), has been well-established in plants (Cui et al., 2015; Jones et al., 2016) and is emerging as an important means to allow the immune system to distinguish pathogens from harmless microbes in animals (Fischer et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Innate immune sensors are under constant selective pressure to adapt due to pathogen evasion or antagonism of immune detection.
source: Complicating the success of host detection systems, innate immune sensors are under constant selective pressure to adapt due to pathogen evasion or antagonism of immune detection.
evidence: This is a general principle in evolutionary immunology supported by established knowledge.

claim: Host-pathogen arms races result from genetic conflicts where both host and pathogen are continually driven to adapt to maintain a fitness advantage.
source: Such evolutionary dynamics, termed host-pathogen arms races, result from genetic conflicts where both host and pathogen are continually driven to adapt to maintain a fitness advantage.
evidence: This is a general principle in evolutionary biology supported by established knowledge.

claim: The antagonistic nature of host-pathogen conflicts can be distinguished via signatures of rapid molecular evolution at the exact sites where host and pathogen interact.
source: The antagonistic nature of these conflicts can be distinguished via signatures of rapid molecular evolution at the exact sites where host and pathogen interact (Daugherty and Malik, 2012; Meyerson and Sawyer, 2011; Sironi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Innate immune sensors of both broad molecular patterns and specific pathogen-associated effectors have been shown to be engaged in genetic conflicts with pathogens.
source: Consistent with their role as the first line of cellular defense against incoming pathogens, innate immune sensors of both broad molecular patterns as well as specific pathogen-associated effectors have been shown to be engaged in genetic conflicts with pathogens (Cagliani et al., 2014; Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016; Hancks et al., 2015; Tenthorey et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inflammasomes are rapidly evolving cytosolic immune sensor complexes.
source: Inflammasomes are one such group of rapidly evolving cytosolic immune sensor complexes (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016; Evavold and Kagan, 2019; Rathinam and Fitzgerald, 2016; Tenthorey et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Upon detection of microbial molecules or pathogen-encoded activities, inflammasome-forming sensor proteins serve as a platform for the recruitment and activation of proinflammatory caspases including caspase-1 (CASP1).
source: Upon detection of microbial molecules or pathogen-encoded activities, inflammasome-forming sensor proteins serve as a platform for the recruitment and activation of proinflammatory caspases including caspase-1 (CASP1) through either a pyrin domain (PYD) or a caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD) (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Rathinam and Fitzgerald, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Active CASP1 mediates the maturation and release of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)−1β and IL-18.
source: Active CASP1 mediates the maturation and release of the proinflammatory cytokines interleukin (IL)−1β and IL-18 (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Rathinam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CASP1 initiates a form of cell death known as pyroptosis.
source: CASP1 also initiates a form of cell death known as pyroptosis (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Rathinam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inflammasome outputs provide robust defense against a wide array of eukaryotic, bacterial, and viral pathogens.
source: Together, these outputs provide robust defense against a wide array of eukaryotic, bacterial, and viral pathogens (Broz and Dixit, 2016; Evavold and Kagan, 2019; Rathinam and Fitzgerald, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NLRP1 is a member of the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing (NLR) superfamily.
source: The first described inflammasome is scaffolded by the sensor protein NLRP1, a member of the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-containing (NLR) superfamily (Martinon et al., 2002; Ting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NLRP1 has an unusual domain architecture, containing a CARD at its C-terminus rather than the N-terminus like all other inflammasome sensor NLRs.
source: NLRP1 has an unusual domain architecture, containing a CARD at its C-terminus rather than the N-terminus like all other inflammasome sensor NLRs, and a function-to-find domain (FIIND), which is located between the LRRs and CARD (Ting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NLRP1 contains a function-to-find domain (FIIND) located between the LRRs and CARD.
source: NLRP1 has an unusual domain architecture, containing a CARD at its C-terminus rather than the N-terminus like all other inflammasome sensor NLRs, and a function-to-find domain (FIIND), which is located between the LRRs and CARD (Ting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The FIIND undergoes a constitutive self-cleavage event.
source: The FIIND undergoes a constitutive self-cleavage event, such that NLRP1 exists in its non-activated state as two, noncovalently associated polypeptides (D'Osualdo et al., 2011; Finger et al., 2012; Frew et al., 2012), the N-terminal domains and the C-terminal CARD-containing fragment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: NLRP1 exists in its non-activated state as two, noncovalently associated polypeptides: the N-terminal domains and the C-terminal CARD-containing fragment.
source: The FIIND undergoes a constitutive self-cleavage event, such that NLRP1 exists in its non-activated state as two, noncovalently associated polypeptides (D'Osualdo et al., 2011; Finger et al., 2012; Frew et al., 2012), the N-terminal domains and the C-terminal CARD-containing fragment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Bacillus anthracis Lethal Toxin (LeTx) is required to elicit a protective inflammatory response against B. anthracis infection via mouse NLRP1B.
source: The first hint that NLRP1 does not detect broadly conserved microbial molecules came from the discovery that the Bacillus anthracis Lethal Toxin (LeTx) is required to elicit a protective inflammatory response against B. anthracis infection via one of the mouse NLRP1 homologs, NLRP1B (Boyden and Dietrich, 2006; Greaney et al., 2020; Moayeri et al., 2010; Terra et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inflammasome activation is the result of site-specific cleavage in the N-terminus of mouse NLRP1B by the Lethal Factor (LF) protease subunit of LeTx.
source: Paradoxically, inflammasome activation is the result of site-specific cleavage in the N-terminus of mouse NLRP1B by the Lethal Factor (LF) protease subunit of LeTx, indicating that protease-mediated cleavage of NLRP1 does not disable its function but instead results in its activation (Chavarría-Smith and Vance, 2013; Levinsohn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Protease-mediated cleavage of NLRP1 does not disable its function but instead results in its activation.
source: Paradoxically, inflammasome activation is the result of site-specific cleavage in the N-terminus of mouse NLRP1B by the Lethal Factor (LF) protease subunit of LeTx, indicating that protease-mediated cleavage of NLRP1 does not disable its function but instead results in its activation (Chavarría-Smith and Vance, 2013; Levinsohn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Proteolysis of mouse NLRP1B by LF results in exposure of a novel N-terminus, which is then targeted for proteasomal degradation by the 'N-end rule' pathway.
source: These studies revealed that proteolysis of mouse NLRP1B by LF results in exposure of a novel N-terminus, which is then targeted for proteasomal degradation by a protein quality control mechanism called the 'N-end rule' pathway (Chui et al., 2019; Sandstrom et al., 2019; Wickliffe et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The proteasome progressively degrades the N-terminal domains of NLRP1B but is disengaged upon arriving at the self-cleavage site within the FIIND domain.
source: Since the proteasome is a processive protease, it progressively degrades the N-terminal domains of NLRP1B but is disengaged upon arriving at the self-cleavage site within the FIIND domain.
evidence: This is supported by prior work on the mechanism of NLRP1B activation.

claim: Degradation of the N-terminal domains releases the bioactive C-terminal CARD-containing fragment of NLRP1B from its non-covalent association with the N-terminal domains, which is sufficient to initiate downstream inflammasome activation.
source: Degradation of the N-terminal domains thus releases the bioactive C-terminal CARD-containing fragment of NLRP1B from its non-covalent association with the N-terminal domains, which is sufficient to initiate downstream inflammasome activation (Chui et al., 2019; Sandstrom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The N-terminal domains of NLRP1 are not required for NLRP1 activation per se, but rather serve a pathogen-sensing function.
source: Such a model indicates that the N-terminal domains are not required for NLRP1 activation per se, but rather serve a pathogen-sensing function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of NLRP1 activation.

claim: The N-terminal 'linker' region in mouse NLRP1B that is cleaved by LF is rapidly evolving in rodents.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminal 'linker' region in mouse NLRP1B that is cleaved by LF is rapidly evolving in rodents, and the analogous linker region is likewise rapidly evolving in primate species (Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The analogous linker region in primate NLRP1 is rapidly evolving.
source: Interestingly, the N-terminal 'linker' region in mouse NLRP1B that is cleaved by LF is rapidly evolving in rodents, and the analogous linker region is likewise rapidly evolving in primate species (Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Selection from pathogens has been driving diversification of the protease target region of NLRP1, possibly serving to bait diverse pathogenic proteases into cleaving NLRP1 and activating the inflammasome responses.
source: These data suggest that selection from pathogens has been driving diversification of this protease target region of NLRP1, possibly serving to bait diverse pathogenic proteases into cleaving NLRP1 and activating the inflammasome responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of evolutionary data that involves speculation about function.

claim: LF neither cleaves nor activates human NLRP1.
source: Consistent with the rapid evolution in NLRP1 at the site of proteolytic cleavage, LF neither cleaves nor activates human NLRP1 (Mitchell et al., 2019; Moayeri et al., 2012; Taabazuing et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Human NLRP1 can be activated by proteolysis when a tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease site is engineered into the rapidly evolving linker region.
source: Despite this, human NLRP1 can also be activated by proteolysis when a tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease site is engineered into the rapidly evolving linker region of human NLRP1 that is analogous to the site of LF cleavage in mouse NLRP1B (Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Human NLRP1 may serve as a 'tripwire' sensor for pathogen-encoded proteases.
source: Thus, like mouse NLRP1B, it has been predicted that human NLRP1 may serve as a 'tripwire' sensor for pathogen-encoded proteases (Mitchell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior work.

claim: Picornaviridae encompass a diverse set of human enteric and respiratory pathogens including coxsackieviruses, polioviruses, and rhinoviruses.
source: We reasoned that human viruses, many of which encode proteases as necessary enzymes for their replication cycle, may be triggers for NLRP1 activation. To pursue this hypothesis, we focused on viruses in the Picornaviridae family, which encompass a diverse set of human enteric and respiratory pathogens including coxsackieviruses, polioviruses, and rhinoviruses (Zell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Picornaviruses translate their genome as a single polyprotein, which is then cleaved into mature proteins in at least six sites in a sequence-specific manner by a virally encoded 3C protease (3Cpro).
source: These viruses all translate their genome as a single polyprotein, which is then cleaved into mature proteins in at least six sites in a sequence-specific manner by a virally encoded 3C protease, termed 3Cpro (Laitinen et al., 2016; Solomon et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2016; Zell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 3Cpro is known to proteolytically target numerous host factors, many of which are associated with immune modulation.
source: 3Cpro is also known to proteolytically target numerous host factors, many of which are associated with immune modulation (Croft et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2015; Lei et al., 2017; Mukherjee et al., 2011; Qian et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Wen et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2014; Xiang et al., 2016; Zaragoza et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 3Cpro are evolutionarily constrained to cleave several specific polyprotein sites and host targets for replicative success.
source: Because 3Cpro are evolutionarily constrained to cleave several specific polyprotein sites and host targets for replicative success, we reasoned that human NLRP1 may have evolved to sense viral infection by mimicking viral polyprotein cleavage sites, leading to NLRP1 cleavage and inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a reasoning based on knowledge of viral protease constraints.

claim: NLRP1 is cleaved in its rapidly evolving linker region by several 3Cpro from picornaviruses, resulting in inflammasome activation.
source: Using an evolution-guided approach, we now show that NLRP1 is cleaved in its rapidly evolving linker region by several 3Cpro from picornaviruses, resulting in inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Human rhinovirus (HRV) 3Cpro cleaves and activates NLRP1 in airway epithelia.
source: These results are consistent with the recent discovery that human rhinovirus (HRV) 3Cpro cleaves and activates NLRP1 in airway epithelia (Robinson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: Variation in the cleavage site among primates leads to changes in cleavage susceptibility and inflammasome activation.
source: We also find that variation in the cleavage site among primates, and even within the human population, leads to changes in cleavage susceptibility and inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Variation in the cleavage site within the human population leads to changes in cleavage susceptibility and inflammasome activation.
source: We also find that variation in the cleavage site among primates, and even within the human population, leads to changes in cleavage susceptibility and inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Proteases from multiple genera of viruses cleave and activate human NLRP1 and mouse NLRP1B at different sites.
source: Interestingly, we observe that proteases from multiple genera of viruses cleave and activate human NLRP1 and mouse NLRP1B at different sites, supporting a role for an evolutionary conflict between viral proteases and NLRP1.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The observation that proteases from multiple genera cleave NLRP1 at different sites supports a role for an evolutionary conflict between viral proteases and NLRP1.
source: Interestingly, we observe that proteases from multiple genera of viruses cleave and activate human NLRP1 and mouse NLRP1B at different sites, supporting a role for an evolutionary conflict between viral proteases and NLRP1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data involving inference about evolutionary conflict.

claim: NLRP1 evolves cleavage motifs that mimic natural sites of proteolytic cleavage in the viral polyprotein.
source: Taken together, our work highlights the role of NLRP1 in sensing and responding to diverse viral proteases by evolving cleavage motifs that mimic natural sites of proteolytic cleavage in the viral polyprotein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The linker in primate NLRP1 has undergone recurrent positive selection.
source: Second, the linker in primate NLRP1, which is analogous to the N-terminal disordered region of NLRP1B that is cleaved by LF protease, has undergone recurrent positive selection (Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016), or an excess of non-synonymous amino acid substitutions over what would be expected by neutral evolution (Kimura, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recurrent positive selection is defined as an excess of non-synonymous amino acid substitutions over what would be expected by neutral evolution.
source: Second, the linker in primate NLRP1, which is analogous to the N-terminal disordered region of NLRP1B that is cleaved by LF protease, has undergone recurrent positive selection (Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016), or an excess of non-synonymous amino acid substitutions over what would be expected by neutral evolution (Kimura, 1983).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claim: The enterovirus 3Cpro cleavage motif is [A/Φ]XXQGXXX (where Φ denotes a hydrophobic residue and X denotes any amino acid).
source: After removing redundant sequences, we used the MEME Suite (Bailey et al., 2009) to create the following 3Cpro cleavage motif: [A/Φ]XXQGXXX (where Φ denotes a hydrophobic residue and X denotes any amino acid), which is broadly consistent with previous studies that have experimentally profiled the substrate specificity of enterovirus 3Cpros (Blom et al., 1996; Fan et al., 2020; Jagdeo et al., 2018; O'Donoghue et al., 2012; Figure 1C).
evidence: This motif was generated from analysis of viral sequences and is consistent with prior experimental work.

claim: The generated 3Cpro cleavage motif is broadly consistent with previous studies that have experimentally profiled the substrate specificity of enterovirus 3Cpros.
source: After removing redundant sequences, we used the MEME Suite (Bailey et al., 2009) to create the following 3Cpro cleavage motif: [A/Φ]XXQGXXX (where Φ denotes a hydrophobic residue and X denotes any amino acid), which is broadly consistent with previous studies that have experimentally profiled the substrate specificity of enterovirus 3Cpros (Blom et al., 1996; Fan et al., 2020; Jagdeo et al., 2018; O'Donoghue et al., 2012; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The 3Cpro cleavage motif was used to successfully predict the site of enterovirus 3Cpro cleavage at position 130–131 within the rapidly-evolving linker of NLRP1.
source: Indeed, by harvesting publicly available enterovirus polyprotein sequences for known 3Cpro cleavage sites, we created a 3Cpro cleavage motif that was used to successfully predict the site of enterovirus 3Cpro cleavage at position 130–131 within the rapidly-evolving linker NLRP1.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental validation.

claim: CVB3 3Cpro cleaves human NLRP1 at the predicted 127-GCTQGSER-134 site.
source: We observed that the WT but not catalytically inactive (C147A) CVB3 3Cpro cleaved NLRP1, resulting in a cleavage product with a molecular weight consistent with our predicted 3Cpro cleavage at the predicted 127-GCTQGSER-134 site (44 kDa) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Catalytically inactive CVB3 3Cpro (C147A) does not cleave NLRP1.
source: We observed that the WT but not catalytically inactive (C147A) CVB3 3Cpro cleaved NLRP1, resulting in a cleavage product with a molecular weight consistent with our predicted 3Cpro cleavage at the predicted 127-GCTQGSER-134 site (44 kDa) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The G131P mutation in NLRP1 abolishes 3Cpro cleavage.
source: To determine if the cleavage occurs between residues 130 and 131, we mutated the P1' glycine to a proline (G131P), which abolished 3Cpro cleavage of NLRP1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CVB3 3Cpro cleavage of NLRP1 is robust and specific.
source: CVB3 3Cpro cleavage of NLRP1 resulted in a similarly intense cleavage product when compared to the previously described system in which a TEV protease site was introduced into the linker region of NLRP1 (Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016; Figure 2D). Taken together, these results indicate that cleavage of WT NLRP1 by a protease from a natural human pathogen is robust and specific.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CVB3 infection results in rapid and specific cleavage of human NLRP1.
source: We observed accumulation of the expected cleavage product beginning at 6 hr post-infection when we infected cells expressing WT NLRP1 and no cleavage product when we infected cells expressing the 131P mutant (Figure 2E). These results validate that CVB3 infection can result in rapid and specific cleavage of human NLRP1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CVB3 3Cpro results in robust NLRP1 inflammasome activation, as measured by CASP1-dependent processing of pro-IL-1β to the active p17 form.
source: We observed that the CVB3 3Cpro results in robust NLRP1 inflammasome activation, as measured by CASP1-dependent processing of pro-IL-1β to the active p17 form (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CVB3 3Cpro activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome is prevented by introduction of a mutation in the NLRP1 FIIND (S1213A).
source: As expected, CVB3 3Cpro activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome was prevented by introduction of a mutation in the NLRP1 FIIND (S1213A) (D'Osualdo et al., 2011; Finger et al., 2012; Frew et al., 2012; Figure 3—figure supplement 1 – panel A), which prevents FIIND auto-processing and the release of the bioactive C-terminal UPA–CARD (Chui et al., 2019; Sandstrom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemical inhibitors of the proteasome (MG132) block CVB3 3Cpro activation of NLRP1.
source: Consistent with recent results (Robinson et al., 2020), we also observed that chemical inhibitors of the proteasome (MG132) or the Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligases that are required for the degradation of proteins with a novel N-terminal glycine (MLN4924) (Timms et al., 2019), also blocked CVB3 3Cpro activation of NLRP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 – panel B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemical inhibitors of Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligases (MLN4924) block CVB3 3Cpro activation of NLRP1.
source: Consistent with recent results (Robinson et al., 2020), we also observed that chemical inhibitors of the proteasome (MG132) or the Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligases that are required for the degradation of proteins with a novel N-terminal glycine (MLN4924) (Timms et al., 2019), also blocked CVB3 3Cpro activation of NLRP1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 – panel B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3Cpro treatment results in release of >4 ng/ml of active IL-1β into the culture supernatant.
source: When compared to a standard curve (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we found that 3Cpro treatment resulted in release of >4 ng/ml of active IL-1β into the culture supernatant (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CVB3 3Cpro cleavage at a single site is both necessary and sufficient to activate NLRP1.
source: Importantly, in both western blot and cell culture assays, 3Cpro-induced inflammasome activation was comparable to TEV-induced activation and was ablated when position 131 was mutated, validating that CVB3 3Cpro cleavage at a single site is both necessary and sufficient to activate NLRP1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: CVB3 3Cpro activates the NLRP1 inflammasome via site-specific cleavage and subsequent 'functional degradation'.
source: Taken together, our results are consistent with CVB3 3Cpro activating the NLRP1 inflammasome via site-specific cleavage and subsequent 'functional degradation' (Chui et al., 2019; Sandstrom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and consistent with prior mechanistic work.

claim: CVB3 infection of inflammasome-reconstituted HEK293T cells results in robust release of active IL-1β when cells were transfected with WT NLRP1 but not the uncleavable mutant NLRP1.
source: Eight hours after infection with CVB3, we observe robust release of active IL-1β into the culture supernatant when cells were transfected with WT NLRP1 but not the uncleavable mutant NLRP1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CVB3 infection of HaCaT human keratinocytes results in a significant increase in supernatant IL-1β that is reduced in cells that lack either NLRP1 or CASP1.
source: Consistent with our model that CVB3 infection cleaves and activates the NLRP1 inflammasome, we observe a significant increase in supernatant IL-1β after CVB3 infection that is reduced in cells that lack either NLRP1 or CASP1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CVB3 infection, through 3Cpro cleavage of the tripwire region of NLRP1, activates the NLRP1 inflammasome.
source: Together, these results indicate that CVB3 infection, through 3Cpro cleavage of the tripwire region of NLRP1, activates the NLRP1 inflammasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Changes in the NLRP1 linker region among primates confer host-specific differences to NLRP1 cleavage and inflammasome activation.
source: Our evolutionary model in which NLRP1 is evolving in conflict with 3Cpro suggests that changes in the NLRP1 linker region, both among primates and within the human population (Figure 4A), would confer host-specific differences to NLRP1 cleavage and inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a prediction that is tested and supported by experimental data.

claim: Changes in the NLRP1 linker region within the human population confer host-specific differences to NLRP1 cleavage and inflammasome activation.
source: Our evolutionary model in which NLRP1 is evolving in conflict with 3Cpro suggests that changes in the NLRP1 linker region, both among primates and within the human population (Figure 4A), would confer host-specific differences to NLRP1 cleavage and inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a prediction that is tested and supported by experimental data.

claim: The human NLRP1 mutants G127E and G131R prevent 3Cpro cleavage of NLRP1.
source: To confirm these predictions, we made the human NLRP1 mutants G127E or G131R, which reflect the Old World monkey or marmoset residues at each position, respectively. As predicted, both primate NLRP1 variants prevented 3Cpro cleavage of NLRP1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Single changes within a short linear motif can substantially alter cleavage susceptibility and inflammasome activation.
source: These results indicate that multiple viral 3Cpro activate host NLRP1 in a host specific manner and suggest that single changes within a short linear motif can substantially alter cleavage susceptibility and inflammasome activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A 3Cpro cleavage site mimic emerged in simian primates 30–40 million years ago.
source: We further observed that this cleavage site is largely absent in non-primate species (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that a 3Cpro cleavage site mimic emerged in simian primates 30–40 million years ago.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: There is weak cleavage of mouse NLRP1B at a site closer to the N-terminus than the 127-GCTQGSER-134 site found in human NLRP1.
source: Despite this, we found that there was weak cleavage of mouse NLRP1B at a site closer to the N-terminus than the 127-GCTQGSER-134 site found in human NLRP1 (Figure 4D and Figure 6A), suggesting that an independent cleavage site could have arisen elsewhere in mouse NLRP1B.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 6A.

claim: NLRP1 in other mammals may have convergently evolved cleavage sites in the linker region despite not having a cleavable sequence in the precise position that human NLRP1 is cleaved.
source: These data suggest that NLRP1 in other mammals may have convergently evolved cleavage sites in the linker region despite not having a cleavable sequence in the precise position that human NLRP1 is cleaved.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data involving inference about convergent evolution.

claim: The Q130R mutation in human NLRP1 (rs150929926) is present in >1 in every 1000 African alleles sampled.
source: While this region does not appear to be highly polymorphic in humans, we note that one alternative allele (rs150929926) results in a Q130R mutation and is present in >1 in every 1000 African alleles sampled.
evidence: This is based on data from GnomAD.

claim: The Q130R mutation in NLRP1 eliminates NLRP1 cleavage susceptibility to CVB3 3Cpro.
source: Introducing this mutation into NLRP1, we find the Q130R mutation eliminates NLRP1 cleavage susceptibility to CVB3 3Cpro (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Loss of cleavage susceptibility results in a loss of inflammasome activation in response to 3Cpro.
source: In the case of primate and human diversity alleles at the site of 3Cpro cleavage, we also find that loss of cleavage susceptibility results in a loss of inflammasome activation in response to 3Cpro (Figure 4F), supporting the aforementioned notion that single changes in the linker region can have drastic impacts on the ability of different hosts to respond to the presence of cytoplasmic 3Cpro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Every tested member of enterovirus 3Cpro was able to cleave NLRP1 between residues 130 and 131.
source: Consistent with this predicted target similarity and prior data with HRV (Robinson et al., 2020), we found that every tested member of enterovirus 3Cpro was able to cleave NLRP1 between residues 130 and 131 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of every tested enterovirus 3Cpro resulted in activation of the inflammasome in a manner that was dependent on cleavage at the 127-GCTQGSER-134 site.
source: Moreover, expression of every tested enterovirus 3Cpro resulted in activation of the inflammasome in a manner that was dependent on cleavage at the 127-GCTQGSER-134 site (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Most picornavirus proteases cleaved human NLRP1 to some degree.
source: Interestingly, we found that there was substantial variation in NLRP1 cleavage sites across these diverse 3Cpro even though most picornavirus proteases cleaved human NLRP1 to some degree (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 3Cpro from EMCV and ParA did not cleave NLRP1.
source: For instance, while 3Cpro from EMCV and ParA did not cleave NLRP1, we observed distinct cleavage sites for 3Cpro from Aichi, HepA, SaliA and Rosa2 (Figure 5B), all of which have at least one cleavage site predicted to occur in the linker region (expected size between 40 kDa and 67 kDa).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 3Cpro from Aichi, HepA, SaliA and Rosa2 have distinct cleavage sites in NLRP1.
source: For instance, while 3Cpro from EMCV and ParA did not cleave NLRP1, we observed distinct cleavage sites for 3Cpro from Aichi, HepA, SaliA and Rosa2 (Figure 5B), all of which have at least one cleavage site predicted to occur in the linker region (expected size between 40 kDa and 67 kDa).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The G131P NLRP1 mutant is still cleaved by the non-enteroviral proteases.
source: Confirming that these proteases cleave at a site that is distinct from that of enteroviruses, the G131P NLRP1 mutant is still cleaved by the non-enteroviral proteases (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only Rosa2 3Cpro was able to activate the NLRP1 inflammasome among the non-enteroviral proteases tested.
source: Surprisingly, when we interrogated NLRP1 inflammasome activation by 3Cpros from Aichi, HepA, SaliA, and Rosa2, all of which robustly cleave NLRP1 at a site in the linker region, we found that only Rosa2 was able to activate the NLRP1 inflammasome (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Co-expression of 3Cpro from Aichi, HepA, SaliA can attenuate NLRP1 activation by TEV protease.
source: Indeed, we find that co-expression of 3Cpro from Aichi, HepA, SaliA can attenuate NLRP1 activation by TEV protease (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), consistent with the idea that these three proteases can actively block NLRP1 activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Non-enteroviral 3Cpros can cleave NLRP1 at independent sites in the rapidly evolving linker region.
source: Nevertheless, our data demonstrate that non-enteroviral 3Cpros can cleave NLRP1 at independent sites in the rapidly evolving linker region and can, in at least one case, activate the human NLRP1 inflammasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There is no cleavage of NLRP1 when cells are infected with EMCV, despite seeing robust cleavage when infected with CVB3.
source: Consistent with our co-transfection experiments, we see no cleavage of NLRP1 when we infect with EMCV, despite seeing robust cleavage when we infect with CVB3 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There is no IL-1β release when cells are infected with EMCV.
source: Likewise, we see no IL-1β release when we infect either inflammasome-reconstituted HEK293T cells or inflammasome-competent HaCaT cells with EMCV (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Evolution of viral 3Cpro cleavage specificity alters whether a virus can be sensed by the NLRP1 tripwire or not.
source: These data indicate that evolution of viral 3Cpro cleavage specificity alters whether a virus can be sensed by the NLRP1 tripwire or not.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Enterovirus 3Cpro cleavage of mouse NLRP1B results in allele-specific cleavage products.
source: Strikingly, when we co-transfected NLRP1B from either the 129 or the B6 strains with diverse enterovirus 3Cpros, we observed allele-specific cleavage products (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 3Cpro from enteroviruses varied substantially in their ability to cleave 129 NLRP1B.
source: Consistent with data in Figure 4D, we observed weak cleavage of 129 NLRP1B by CVB3 3Cpro. In addition, we found that 3Cpro from other enteroviruses varied substantially in their ability to cleave 129 NLRP1B, including no detectable cleavage with EV71 3Cpro and a different dominant position of cleavage by HRV 3Cpro.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Enterovirus 3Cpro cleavage of 129 NLRP1B results in weak cleavage and little to no inflammasome activation.
source: Despite this variation, we only observed weak cleavage (Figure 6A, left) and little to no inflammasome activation (Figure 6B, left) by any enterovirus 3Cpros tested against 129 NLRP1B.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Enterovirus 3Cpro cleavage of B6 NLRP1B results in a consistent-sized cleavage product across all enterovirus 3Cpros.
source: In contrast, enterovirus 3Cpro cleavage of B6 NLRP1B resulted in a consistent-sized cleavage product across all enterovirus 3Cpros that ranged in intensities between the different viral proteases, more similar to our observations with human NLRP1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Co-transfection with HRV 3Cpro results in a very strong cleavage product, almost complete loss of full length B6 NLRP1B, and very strong activation of the inflammasome.
source: Most interestingly, we observed that co-transfection with HRV 3Cpro resulted in the appearance of a very strong cleavage product (Figure 6A, right), almost complete loss of full length B6 NLRP1B (Figure 6A and B, right) and very strong activation of the inflammasome (Figure 6B, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Mouse NLRP1B can be cleaved and activated by viral proteases.
source: These data indicate that mouse NLRP1B can also be cleaved and activated by viral proteases, which suggests that the evolution of the N-terminus of NLRP1B between closely related mouse strains (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) is not only shaping susceptibility to tripwire cleavage by the bacterial LF protease, but also impacts tripwire cleavage by viral 3Cpros.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The evolution of the N-terminus of NLRP1B between closely related mouse strains is shaping susceptibility to tripwire cleavage by both bacterial LF protease and viral 3Cpros.
source: These data indicate that mouse NLRP1B can also be cleaved and activated by viral proteases, which suggests that the evolution of the N-terminus of NLRP1B between closely related mouse strains (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) is not only shaping susceptibility to tripwire cleavage by the bacterial LF protease, but also impacts tripwire cleavage by viral 3Cpros.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Both host and viral evolution shape the outcome of the interaction between NLRP1 and 3Cpro.
source: Taken together, these data further support the model in which both host and viral evolution, even within closely related host and viral species, shape the outcome of the interaction between NLRP1 and 3Cpro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Molecular mimicry of host proteins is commonly deployed by pathogens to antagonize host defenses.
source: For instance, molecular mimicry of host proteins is commonly deployed by pathogens to antagonize host defenses, as it limits the evolutionary options for the host to counter-evolve (Elde and Malik, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pathogens can mimic 'short linear motifs' (SLIMs) through evolution of only a small number of amino acids to hijack highly conserved host processes.
source: Beyond mimicry of entire proteins or protein domains, pathogens can also mimic so-called 'short linear motifs' (SLIMs) through evolution of only a small number of amino acids to hijack highly conserved host processes such as post-translational modifications or binding by small protein domains (Chemes et al., 2015; Hagai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Changing protease specificity requires concomitant changes to several independent cleavage sites, which is difficult to accomplish in a single evolutionary step.
source: Thus, changing protease specificity requires concomitant changes to several independent cleavage sites, which is difficult to accomplish in a single evolutionary step.
evidence: This is a reasoning based on knowledge of viral evolution.

claim: Protease cleavage motifs often only span a small number of amino acids, potentially facilitating the independent evolution of these SLIMs in host proteins.
source: On top of that, protease cleavage motifs often only span a small number of amino acids (Schechter and Berger, 1967), potentially facilitating the independent evolution of these SLIMs in host proteins.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: NLRP1 serves as a sensor for diverse proteases from the Picornaviridae family of human pathogens by mimicking the highly conserved protease cleavage sites found within the viral polyproteins.
source: Here, we show that the inflammasome protein, NLRP1, serves as a sensor for diverse proteases from the Picornaviridae family of human pathogens by mimicking the highly conserved protease cleavage sites found within the viral polyproteins.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: By exploiting a constrained feature of viral evolution and tying it to a pro-inflammatory immune response, NLRP1 allows the immune system to recognize and respond to a wide range of viral proteases expressed in the host cytoplasm.
source: By exploiting a constrained feature of viral evolution and tying it to a pro-inflammatory immune response, such a system allows the immune system to recognize and respond to a wide range of viral proteases expressed in the host cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: NLRP1 represents one of the few known cases of mammalian ETI.
source: NLRP1 represents one of the few known cases of mammalian ETI (Cui et al., 2015; Fischer et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2016), where pathogen-mediated cleavage of NLRP1 promotes its activation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: By holding the small C-terminal CARD-containing fragment in a non-covalent association with the larger N-terminal fragment, the majority of the NLRP1 protein can serve as a sensor for pathogen-encoded effectors.
source: By holding the small C-terminal CARD-containing fragment in a non-covalent association with the larger N-terminal fragment, the majority of the protein can serve as a sensor for pathogen-encoded effectors (Mitchell et al., 2019; Taabazuing et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mouse NLRP1B is specifically cleaved by the protease-containing secreted effector from B. anthracis (LF).
source: Indeed, mouse NLRP1B has been shown to be specifically cleaved by the protease-containing secreted effector from B. anthracis (LF) as well as being ubiquitylated by an E3-ubiquitin ligase from S. flexneri (IpaH7.8) (Sandstrom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mouse NLRP1B is ubiquitylated by an E3-ubiquitin ligase from S. flexneri (IpaH7.8).
source: Indeed, mouse NLRP1B has been shown to be specifically cleaved by the protease-containing secreted effector from B. anthracis (LF) as well as being ubiquitylated by an E3-ubiquitin ligase from S. flexneri (IpaH7.8) (Sandstrom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Proteases from diverse picornaviruses, including CVB3, HRV, EV68, PV1 and Rosa2, specifically cleave several independently evolved sites in human NLRP1, leading to activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β.
source: We now show, using an evolution-guided approach, that proteases from diverse picornaviruses, including human pathogens such as coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3), human rhinovirus A (HRV), enterovirus D68 (EV68) and poliovirus 1 (PV1) and rosavirus A2 (Rosa2), specifically cleave several independently evolved sites in human NLRP1, leading to activation of the NLRP1 inflammasome and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The unique domain architecture of NLRP1 allows the N-terminal linker of human NLRP1 to freely evolve to be recognized by pathogenic effectors.
source: We previously speculated that the unique domain architecture of NLRP1 would allow the N-terminal linker of human NLRP1 to freely evolve to be recognized by pathogenic effectors.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior work.

claim: Human NLRP1 serves as a general enteroviral protease sensor by encoding a polyprotein cleavage site mimic.
source: Additionally, our finding that numerous enteroviruses also cleave at the Q130-G131 site and activate pro-inflammatory cytokine release suggests that human NLRP1 serves as a general enteroviral protease sensor by encoding a polyprotein cleavage site mimic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: NLRP1 sensing of enteroviruses at the Q130-G131 site is an innovation in the primate lineage.
source: Our phylogenetic assessment of the Q130-G131 3Cpro cleavage site in NLRP1 suggests that NLRP1 sensing of enteroviruses at this specific site is an innovation in the primate lineage, and is largely absent in all other mammalian lineages with exception of a possible independent acquisition by members within the Caprinae subfamily of mammals (e.g. goats, sheep) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: In human skin keratinocytes, all components of the NLRP1 inflammasome are basally expressed and thus poised to elicit an inflammatory response.
source: In human skin keratinocytes, where NLRP1 is regarded as the key inflammasome, all components of the NLRP1 inflammasome are basally expressed and thus poised to elicit an inflammatory response (Zhong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Germline mutations in NLRP1 that result in overactivation can cause growth of warts in the upper airway in a condition known as recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JRRP).
source: Here, germline mutations in NLRP1 that result in overactivation can cause growth of warts in the upper airway in a condition known as recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JRRP) (Drutman et al., 2019) and an increase in skin cancer susceptibility and skin disorders such as multiple self-healing palmoplantar carcinoma (MSPC), familial keratosis lichenoides chronica (FKLC) and auto-inflammation with arthritis and dyskeratosis (AIADK) (Grandemange et al., 2017; Herlin et al., 2020; Soler et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Germline mutations in NLRP1 that result in overactivation can cause an increase in skin cancer susceptibility and skin disorders such as MSPC, FKLC and AIADK.
source: Here, germline mutations in NLRP1 that result in overactivation can cause growth of warts in the upper airway in a condition known as recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (JRRP) (Drutman et al., 2019) and an increase in skin cancer susceptibility and skin disorders such as multiple self-healing palmoplantar carcinoma (MSPC), familial keratosis lichenoides chronica (FKLC) and auto-inflammation with arthritis and dyskeratosis (AIADK) (Grandemange et al., 2017; Herlin et al., 2020; Soler et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: dsRNA can activate the NLRP1 inflammasome in human keratinocytes.
source: Additional recent work has indicated that dsRNA can also activate the NLRP1 inflammasome in human keratinocytes (Bauernfried et al., 2020), adding to the role that NLRP1 may play in the inflammatory response.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: NLRP1 is basally expressed in tissues such as the gut and brain.
source: Beyond the skin, NLRP1 is also basally expressed in tissues such as the gut and brain (D'Osualdo et al., 2015; Kaushal et al., 2015; Kummer et al., 2007), which are sites of picornavirus replication where overactivation upon infection may result in immunopathology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 3Cpros from nearly every genus of human-infecting picornavirus can cleave NLRP1 somewhere in the rapidly evolving linker region between the PYD and NLR domain.
source: Intriguingly, 3Cpros from nearly every genus of human-infecting picornavirus can cleave NLRP1 somewhere in the rapidly evolving linker region between the PYD and NLR domain, although only enteroviruses cleave at the specific site between position 130 and 131.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Only enteroviruses cleave NLRP1 at the specific site between position 130 and 131.
source: Intriguingly, 3Cpros from nearly every genus of human-infecting picornavirus can cleave NLRP1 somewhere in the rapidly evolving linker region between the PYD and NLR domain, although only enteroviruses cleave at the specific site between position 130 and 131.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The extended linker region of NLRP1 may be convergently evolving to mimic cleavage sites from a diverse range of viruses at multiple independent sites.
source: These data suggest that this extended linker, which we previously found showed widespread signatures of positive selection (Chavarría-Smith et al., 2016), may be convergently evolving to mimic cleavage sites from a diverse range of viruses at multiple independent sites.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data involving inference about convergent evolution.

claim: Multiple viral proteases cleave mouse NLRP1B at different sites within NLRP1 in a strain-specific manner.
source: Supporting that model, we observe a similar phenomenon in mouse NLRP1B, where multiple viral proteases cleave at different sites within NLRP1 in a strain-specific manner.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Not all cleavage events by 3Cpro lead to inflammasome activation in the same way that enteroviral cleavage does.
source: Intriguingly, not all these cleavage events lead to inflammasome activation in the same way that enteroviral cleavage does, and we find evidence for antagonism of NLRP1 activation by some 3Cpros, suggesting that additional activities of 3Cpro may be the next step in the arms race, serving to prevent inflammasome activation even after the tripwire has been tripped.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: There is evidence for antagonism of NLRP1 activation by some 3Cpros.
source: Intriguingly, not all these cleavage events lead to inflammasome activation in the same way that enteroviral cleavage does, and we find evidence for antagonism of NLRP1 activation by some 3Cpros, suggesting that additional activities of 3Cpro may be the next step in the arms race, serving to prevent inflammasome activation even after the tripwire has been tripped.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Additional activities of 3Cpro may be the next step in the arms race, serving to prevent inflammasome activation even after the tripwire has been tripped.
source: Intriguingly, not all these cleavage events lead to inflammasome activation in the same way that enteroviral cleavage does, and we find evidence for antagonism of NLRP1 activation by some 3Cpros, suggesting that additional activities of 3Cpro may be the next step in the arms race, serving to prevent inflammasome activation even after the tripwire has been tripped.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Host mimicry of viral polyprotein cleavage motifs could be an important evolutionary strategy in the ongoing arms race between host and viruses.
source: Taken together, our work suggests that host mimicry of viral polyprotein cleavage motifs could be an important evolutionary strategy in the ongoing arms race between host and viruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: One explanation for the observation that the specificity of viral proteases changes within a viral family is that there is evolutionary pressure from the host to evolve cleavage sites and protease specificity.
source: Indeed, one explanation for the somewhat surprising observation that the specificity of viral proteases changes at all within a viral family such as the picornaviruses is that there is evolutionary pressure from the host to evolve cleavage sites and protease specificity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Viral proteases can play roles in antagonizing host immune factors and driving host evolution to avoid being cleaved.
source: Prior work has highlighted the roles that viral proteases can play in antagonizing host immune factors and driving host evolution to avoid being cleaved (Patel et al., 2012; Stabell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mimicry coupled with cleavage-activating immunity as seen with NLRP1 could be a strong pressure to shape the protease specificity.
source: However, mimicry coupled with cleavage-activating immunity as seen with NLRP1 could be an even stronger pressure to shape the protease specificity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Host processes may drive the type of functional diversification of viral protease specificity observed in order to avoid cleaving NLRP1 and other similar ETI factors.
source: By turning the tables, these host processes may drive the type of functional diversification of viral protease specificity that we observe in order to avoid cleaving NLRP1 and other similar ETI factors.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: This evolutionary strategy may be more broadly deployed at other sites of host-pathogen conflicts.
source: We expect that this work may lead to the discovery that such an evolutionary strategy may be more broadly deployed at other sites of host-pathogen conflicts.
evidence: This is a speculation about future discoveries.
